items.excerpt: 「ミッシング・ピーシズ」シリーズ新展開。〈ジュブナイル・ワークス〉と名付け、少年・少⼥向けに描かれた〈⽩⼿塚〉とでも呼びたい作品を収蔵。戦災孤児マサヤンとムギヤンの成長譚を描いた表題作「アリと巨人」。こちらの超入手困難であった1961年中一コース収録オリジナル版の初収録が目玉と言える。他に学園もの「机の中へこんにちは」、ネコ型宇宙人の「シャミー1000」、さらに初単行本化内容を含む「オズマ隊長 防衛博を行く」「ぼくの夢 とんだ宇宙旅行」を併録。少年少女向けだからこそ手塚の想い・哲学が随所に込められており、また60年代ならではのイキのいい描線と作画を体感しつつ当時の空気感をぜひ味わって欲しい作品。

items.body: Label: Biophilia Records, 2026 Personnel - Linda May Han Oh: double bass; Melissa Aldana: tenor saxophone. Bassist Linda May Han Oh and saxophonist Melissa Aldana are two respected bandleaders and composers with different styles and approaches but common journeys in life. Oh was born in Malaysia to parents of Chinese heritage, was raised in Australia, and moved to New York for a brilliant career, having played with Pat Metheny, Vijay Iyer, Joe Lovano, and Dave Douglas, among many others. Aldana is a native of Santiago, Chile, and has lived in New York since 2009, after graduating from Berklee College of Music. For this session, the duo agreed to play standards, showcasing reverence for jazz tradition and influences while also allowing new possibilities to emerge from the arrangements. Yet Beneath Lifted Skies also includes three duo improvisations and three solo bass tracks. Charlie Parker’s “ Anthropology ” comes out of the gate with a vibrantly swinging mood, swift unisons, and exciting exchanges infused with a richness of ideas. Yet it doesn’t beat the fantastic rendition of Bud Powell’s “ Hallucinations ”, where the duo is at its best. Impressive synchronization, great melody, and a grooving, energizing vibe are part of a breathtaking interplay that demonstrates Oh’s immaculate technique and Aldana’s fluid language. Ballads where melody reigns, such as Charles Mingus’ “ Duke Ellington’s Sound of Love ” and Sammy Fain’s “ I’ll Be Seeing You ”, make a great pair. Aldana’s quick-witted, arpeggiated sequences à la Charles Lloyd put a smokiness in the air. In turn, pieces by jazz giants Wayne Shorter (“ Dance Cadaverous ”) and John Coltrane (“ 26-2 ”) didn’t impress me as much. One that really gets under the skin is Gigi Gryce’s “ Social Call ”, a graceful, easy-rolling tune expressed with joyful hookiness. Of the three improvised pieces, “ Infinite ” is the one that caught my ear instantly, relying on droning pedals and searching melodies to take us to a progressive yet atmospheric place. “ Resolve ”, which ends with a pedaling bass figure, also makes for a compelling abstract sonic painting. Oh absolutely excels on her solo reframing of Herbie Hancock’s “ The Sorcerer ”, where edginess and roundness go together, creating an almost subliminal pulse. The bassist also tackles Billie Holiday’s “ God Bless the Child ”, delivered as a protest against child abuse, and introduces a new composition, “ Winter ”, where she employs expert pulses and slides to add novelty. Demonstrating a quick-witted rapport, Oh and Aldana are two kindred spirits in conversation. They’ve already found their own voices in jazz, but together, they manage to offer a very enjoyable album with varied rhythm, groove, and breath. While old standards can sometimes feel stale, creative reinvention transforms them into a thrilling experience. Beneath Lifted Skies is an excellent case in point. Favorite Tracks: 02 - Hallucinations ► 03 - Improvisation: Infinite ► 06 - The Sorcerer ► 10 - Social Call

items.body:
After more than seven decades, Columbia House is calling it a day.

The long-running mail-order media club will stop accepting new orders after 15 September, according to a notice on its website. Customers will still be able to purchase books using existing credits or credit cards.

The closure brings an end to a 71-year run for a company that once changed how millions of people discovered and bought music from home.

Founded in 1955 as the Columbia Record Club by CBS/Columbia Records, the service offered records through the mail, allowing listeners to build their collections without heading to a record store. By 1963, it reportedly accounted for 10% of the music retail market.

Columbia House later expanded its catalogue by licensing releases from other labels and evolved alongside the formats music fans were buying, from vinyl records to cassettes and CDs.

For a generation of listeners, the company became synonymous with offers promising a stack of albums for next to nothing — including its memorable deal of as many as 12 CDs for a penny. The catch was that members would subsequently purchase releases at full price, with the service also using a controversial practice known as “negative option billing”, under which customers could be charged for selections unless they opted out.

At its height in 1996, Columbia House counted 16 million members. That same year, it launched its website as music retail began its shift online.

The decades that followed were considerably rockier. Sony sold half of Columbia House to Time Warner in 1991, while subsequent years saw the company change hands multiple times as online retailers, big-box stores and digital music reshaped the way audiences bought and consumed music.

Competitor BMG acquired Columbia House in 2005 and consolidated its operations. Following another acquisition in 2008, the business was renamed Direct Brands, which eventually ended its music mail-order operations while continuing to sell DVDs and Blu-rays under the Columbia House name.

Its Canadian operation ceased business in 2010, while the US company filed for bankruptcy in 2015. Plans were later floated to revive Columbia House as a vinyl subscription service amid the format's resurgence, but the comeback did not materialise.

Sony Music continues to own the Columbia House trademark, while Edge Line Ventures LLC is its current licensee.

For music fans who remember leafing through catalogues and choosing which albums would arrive at their doorstep next, Columbia House's closure marks the end of a distinctly pre-streaming way of discovering and collecting music.

Music, food, and giving back are coming together at Marina Bay Sands this August. Sands for Singapore Charity Festival is returning for its 12th edition, with its main festivities taking over Event Plaza from 28 to 30 August.

The three-night waterfront celebration will bring together live performances, food pop-ups, community booths, and fundraising activities, with Singaporean musicians taking the stage throughout the weekend.

RRILEY will headline the Festival's opening night on 28 August. The Singaporean artist, who first made her debut as a founding member of local pop quartet The Sam Willows, will perform alongside Thye Hua Kwan Moral Charities' Brave Hearts Ensemble, an inclusive performing arts group formed by residents of THK Home for the Disabled at Eunos.

Local bands 53A, The Vibes, and SuperSonic will also soundtrack the weekend with live renditions of cover favourites.

Beyond the music, festival-goers can head to the Good Bites Market, where five gourmet pop-up experiences will raise funds for non-profit organisation AWWA and its Enabled Living @ Bedok programme, which aims to empower individuals with disabilities to live independently.

Black Tap Craft Burgers & Beer, Bread Street Kitchen, and RISE will serve up specially priced dishes and drinks, while Roberta's Pizza and homegrown Café Nesuto will join the Festival for the first time.

Black Tap Craft Burgers & Beer;The All-American Burger

Visitors can also participate in Impact Match, an interactive game where players create digital school packs containing essential supplies. Each successfully completed pack will be matched by Marina Bay Sands with a school pack for students at NorthLight School.

Meanwhile, the Giving Marketplace will bring together local non-profits, social enterprises, and small businesses, including APSN, ART:DIS, Cat Welfare Society, MINDS, Carer, Social Gifting, Teddy Thotz, and more.

The annual Community Chest Heartstrings Walk and Race to the Sky Vertical Marathon will also return on 29 August. Co-organised by Marina Bay Sands and Community Chest, the event includes a walk around Marina Bay and a 57-storey vertical climb to the SkyPark Observation Deck, supporting more than 300 social service programmes across Singapore.

Giving Marketplace

Dine for Good returns throughout August

The Festival's fundraising efforts will extend beyond Event Plaza with Dine for Good, which runs from 1 to 30 August.

12 signature and celebrity chef restaurants at Marina Bay Sands will each dedicate proceeds from a selected dish to AWWA's Enabled Living @ Bedok programme.

Among the dishes on offer are LAVO's Reginette Seafood Alfredo at S$45++, Yardbird's Chicken & Waffles at S$48++, Maison Boulud's Coq Au Vin at S$42++, and Origin + Bloom's Chicken Rendang Sandwich at S$12 nett.

LAVO Coastal Italian Restaurant and Rooftop Bar; Reginette Seafood Alfredo

Miracle Coffee will also collaborate with Marina Bay Sands' pastry team on a KIKU-inspired matcha and yuzu cake, available exclusively from 10 to 30 August.

Speaking about the initiative, Huixia See Toh, Director of Family Services at AWWA, said: “We look forward to this continued support for AWWA’s latest initiative, Enabled Living @ Bedok, which will empower persons with disabilities to live independently and participate actively in the community with confidence and dignity.”

Since launching in 2013, Sands for Singapore Charity Festival has helped raise more than S$45 million for social causes in Singapore, supporting low-income families, youths, seniors, and persons with disabilities.

“By connecting these experiences with opportunities to give back, we hope to inspire even more people to support causes that matter to Singapore while strengthening the social bonds that help communities thrive,” said Paul Town, Chief Operating Officer at Marina Bay Sands.

items.body:
Singapore-based live entertainment platform Triangle Group has raised US$15 million in funding as it looks to make touring across Asia-Pacific easier for artists and their teams.

The investment comprises a US$10 million equity seed round led by DSG Consumer Partners and US$5 million in venture debt from Genesis Alternative Ventures.

Headquartered in Singapore, Triangle Group currently operates across 18 cities in nine countries, with teams in Singapore, Australia, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Its goal is to tackle one of the longstanding challenges of touring Asia-Pacific: connecting individual markets into viable regional touring routes.

For artists with established fanbases in Asia, mounting a multi-city tour can involve navigating different promoters, visa requirements, tax systems, languages, and audience spending power from market to market.

Zaran Vacha

“Every city in Asia is completely different,” shared Triangle Group co-founder Zaran Vachha. “When we send a proposal to a London agent, they're dealing with one counterparty who actually knows Jakarta, Manila, and Melbourne.”

Vachha has spent two decades developing touring circuits across Asia, working with acts ranging from Pharrell Williams to underground electronic artists. He is joined by co-founder Greg Hargrave, an Australian entrepreneur with experience in fintech and ASX-listed companies, and Chief Financial Officer Matthew Qi-Tao.

The company has also brought former Live Nation Asia Pacific President Roger Field onboard as Executive Director and Operating Partner. Field previously served as CEO of Live Nation Australia & New Zealand and spent a year as an advisor and investor in Triangle before joining the company full-time.

“Running Live Nation across this region taught me one thing: Asia-Pacific doesn't need a global template; it needs an operator who understands every market individually,” said Field.

Roger Field

“That's the business we're building at Triangle—applying global standards with a regional focus. There's a larger piece of the pie we can claim by making it genuinely easier to tour the region.”

Triangle operates a portfolio of live entertainment brands, including Collective Minds, Curious, and Touch Bass.

Collective Minds has worked on tours and events featuring artists including Fred again.., Jamie xx, Charlotte de Witte, Black Coffee, Kamasi Washington, Eric Prydz, and Wolf Alice, alongside festival properties such as A State of Trance (ASOT) and S2O.

Curious focuses on live speaking tours and recently brought The Diary of a CEO author Steven Bartlett to Asia, while Touch Bass operates a multi-city drum & bass touring festival in Australia.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Pitch Control (@pitchcontrolau)

Triangle's wider touring roster has also included HONNE, Hanumankind, Gilles Peterson, James Hype, and Boris Brejcha, among others.

Upcoming events under the group's brands include Singapore shows from The Martinez Brothers, ARTBAT, Intercell, and Dom Dolla, alongside Intercell in Hong Kong and Otherworld Festival in Manila. Its Australian operations also have Tomorrowland CORE in Melbourne and Rampage dates across Australia and New Zealand on the calendar.

According to Triangle Group, Asia-Pacific's live entertainment market is projected to reach US$75 billion by 2033, while the region is expected to account for almost two-thirds of the world's middle class by 2035.

With its latest funding, the company is positioning itself around that growing appetite for live experiences — building the regional infrastructure to make more Asia-Pacific tour stops commercially and operationally possible for artists.

Taipei is gearing up for four days of music, industry exchange, and cross-border discovery as TAIPEI MUSIC EXPO (TMEX) returns to Taipei Music Center from 27 to 30 August.

Held under the theme "Tune in to Taiwan. Sync with Asia.", this year's edition will bring together more than 100 music industry professionals from 15 markets alongside over 60 exhibiting brands from across the region. TMEX will also run alongside its music festival, JAM JAM ASIA, which takes over the weekend of 29 and 30 August with more than 80 acts from 14 markets performing across seven stages.

The expo continues its focus on connecting Taiwan's music scene with the wider Asia-Pacific and global music industries through five pillars: brand exhibitions, business matching, forums, emerging talent showcases, and fan engagement. The first two days will be reserved for industry delegates before the programme opens to the public over the weekend.

TMEX's wider platform is designed to bring artists, audiences, and markets together through its exhibition, forum, festival, and networking programmes, with technology and sustainability identified as key areas of focus.

The team behind KPop Demon Hunters comes to Taipei

Among the highlights of this year's TMEX Forum is a session featuring members of the team behind Netflix's KPop Demon Hunters.

Director Maggie Kang, producer Michelle Wong, and THEBLACKLABEL songwriter Danny Chung, who is also the voice of Baby Saja, will discuss what the film could mean for Asia-Pacific artists looking to enter global markets.

Grammy-winning mastering engineer Howie Weinberg will also make his Taiwan debut with a session exploring the sonic aesthetics behind his work across 9,000 records.

Elsewhere, festival programmers from the US, UK, Korea, Japan, and Taiwan will come together to discuss how festivals develop their identities, audiences, and international partnerships. Other sessions will tackle generative AI in music production with Suno and KKBOX, international artist marketing, and sustainability in live events.

Beyond the forum, TMEX will connect artists and music businesses with international curators and buyers, bringing together festivals, labels, management companies, digital platforms, and music-related brands.

This year's participating organisations include Goldenvoice, Live Nation, Fuji Rock Festival, Summer Sonic, YG PLUS, Zandari Festa, MPMG, Zepp, Beggars Group, and Secretly Group. Music export agencies will also join the exhibition floor, including Thailand's Creative Economy Agency, Vietnam Cultural Industry Development Association, Sounds Australia, and Taiwan's TAICCA.

JAM JAM ASIA brings over 80 acts to seven stages

For fans, the weekend belongs to JAM JAM ASIA.

Taking place across 29 and 30 August, the festival will feature more than 80 acts from 14 markets, spanning everything from Japanese city pop and Indonesian metal to Thai indie and Kazakh electronic music. Performances will unfold across seven stages, including four indoor air-conditioned halls, a 3,000-capacity outdoor stage, free stages spotlighting emerging artists, and late-night DJ takeovers.

Leading the lineup is Japanese city pop pioneer Taeko Onuki, alongside HYUKOH, who will perform with Kuo of Sunset Rollercoaster.

Also joining the bill are Filipino-American neo-soul artist ((( O ))), Indonesian metal trio Voice of Baceprot, Bangkok rapper Réjizz, Korean-Australian rap collective 1300, Seoul indie band HOA, Japanese four-piece ATARASHII GAKKO!, and Japanese hip-hop producer DJ KRUSH.

Taiwan's own scene will also be represented by acts including Elephant Gym and Amazing Show, while JAM JAM ASIA's international partnerships will bring additional cross-border showcase acts to Taipei, including TV Tairiku Ondo via Fuji Rock Festival.

With its mix of industry conversations, international networking, emerging talent, and a sprawling weekend festival, TMEX is positioning Taipei as a meeting point for music scenes from across the Asia-Pacific.

CORTIS have wrapped their first-ever North American tour on a high, selling out every stop of 2026 CORTIS TOUR IN NORTH AMERICA, also known as PUT YOUR PHONE DOWN.

The five-piece — MARTIN, JAMES, JUHOON, SEONGHYEON, and KEONHO — closed out the Live Nation-promoted run with two sold-out nights in San Francisco on 15 and 16 August, following shows in Toronto, New York, Atlanta, Irving, and Los Angeles.

Built around the idea of being fully present at a live show, PUT YOUR PHONE DOWN encouraged fans to experience CORTIS beyond their screens. The concept extended to the group's "PYPD" app, which captured fans' movement and energy throughout the concerts while encouraging them to jump and move along with the performance.

The shows also brought CORTIS closer to their fans, with the members stepping offstage to perform within the crowd. Each stop featured its own touches, including the group sporting cowboy hats during their Irving show.

Across the tour, CORTIS performed tracks including 'YOUNGCREATORCREW', 'FaSHioN', 'REDRED', 'ACAI', 'JoyRide', 'Lullaby', and 'Blue Lips'. Their Juicy J collaboration, 'MOTION (feat. Juicy J)', also made the setlist after receiving its live debut at Lollapalooza Chicago.

The tour followed CORTIS' Lollapalooza Chicago debut on 1 August, where they took over the T-Mobile Stage in front of approximately 50,000 festivalgoers. Clips from the rain-soaked performance gained traction online and helped introduce the group to new audiences.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Lollapalooza (@lollapalooza)

CORTIS have since become the fastest K-pop group to reach 15 million Instagram followers. The group have also amassed 16.3 million followers on TikTok and 6.3 million YouTube subscribers, which BIGHIT MUSIC says are the highest figures among K-pop boy groups that debuted within the past five years.

The momentum has carried over to the charts. CORTIS' second EP, GREENGREEN, jumped 75 places on the Billboard 200, moving from No. 114 to No. 39 in its 13th week on the chart.

Following their North American run, CORTIS will celebrate their first anniversary with the 2026 CORTIS TOUR BIRTHDAY PARTY on 22 and 23 August in Seoul.

The group are also set to return to Southeast Asia later this year, taking the stage at the Formula 1 Singapore Grand Prix on 9 October.

items.body:
The Recording Academy has signalled that it may reconsider its newly introduced Asian Pop GRAMMY category, following criticism from artists and BTS' decision not to submit their music for the upcoming awards.

Recording Academy CEO Harvey Mason Jr. addressed concerns surrounding the category in a statement, acknowledging that some artists do not feel adequately represented by the award.

“It’s clear from our numerous conversations with many stakeholders over the past two weeks that, regardless of our intent and desire to be even more inclusive, there are some artists in this space who feel that this category isn’t representing the music they work so hard to create, in the way they wish,” Mason said in a statement to Billboard.

“As a musician myself, I take that to heart.”

According to Variety, Mason and other GRAMMY executives have been holding discussions with artists and industry representatives across K-pop, J-pop, C-pop, Indian music, and other Asian music communities. The Recording Academy is also reportedly convening its full Board and Awards & Nominations Committee to seek further input on the category and the process through which new GRAMMY categories are introduced.

The development comes after BTS announced on 29 July that they would not submit their music for GRAMMY consideration. In identical statements shared by the members, the group expressed their hope that “music can be heard and loved by itself rather than being divided by region or language.”

The statement was widely interpreted as criticism of the GRAMMYs' new Asian Pop category, which was introduced amid the continued global growth of music from Asia.

The category has since sparked debate over whether creating a region-specific award provides greater representation for Asian artists or instead separates them from established genre and General Field categories. Reports noted that genre-specific categories can face similar criticism when artists feel they are being confined to a particular classification rather than being considered alongside the wider field.

While the Recording Academy has yet to announce any official changes, Mason said its management and Board were committed to ensuring the artists the GRAMMYs intended to recognise “feel truly seen and heard by our actions.”

The Academy's response marks the latest development in the conversation surrounding Asian music's place within major global awards institutions — and whether increasingly borderless pop music should continue to be classified according to geography.

BLACKPINK have addressed fans following criticism surrounding the K-pop group’s 10th anniversary celebrations, with JISOO, ROSÉ, LISA, and JENNIE each sharing messages with BLINKs after the milestone.

The quartet marked their 10th anniversary on 8 August, a decade after making their debut. However, what was meant to be a celebratory moment became a source of disappointment for some fans, who raised concerns over the scale, organisation, and communication surrounding the anniversary activities.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by BLΛƆKPIИK (@blackpinkofficial)

At the centre of the criticism was an anniversary event held at the National Museum of Korea in Seoul’s Yongsan District. According to reports, the event was announced two days beforehand and was attended by 40 fans selected from paid Weverse membership holders.

All four BLACKPINK members ultimately attended the gathering, which included interactions with fans, flowers, and a three-tiered pink cake. The group also appeared together for a brief livestream.

However, the relatively intimate scale of the event — alongside earlier uncertainty over whether all four members would be present and the limited advance notice — left some BLINKs disappointed. Reports described the livestream as lasting around 10 minutes and the main programme around 30 minutes.

JISOO addresses BLINKs during anniversary celebrations

[TRANS] jisoo: We really wanted to meet a lot of fans, and we know how important our 10th anniversary is. But I think there were some issues with our communication and we’re very sorry about that. We really wanted to spend the day happily with joy and we want to say that we…

— BLACKPINK BLINK UNION 💕 (@BBU_BLACKPINK) August 8, 2026

JISOO was among the first members to address the response from fans.

During the livestream, she acknowledged that communication surrounding the anniversary could have been better and apologised to BLINKs who had been left disappointed.

“I originally wanted to see so many of you, and I knew this was an important day — our 10th anniversary,” she said. “I wanted this to be a happy occasion, but I’m sorry to the BLINKs who feel let down. I hope you know that I love you.”

After footage of JISOO becoming emotional while reading fan letters prompted speculation online, she later asked fans to refrain from negative discussion and “baseless speculation” surrounding the anniversary.

ROSÉ says she wanted the anniversary to be a day everyone could celebrate

ROSÉ subsequently shared a longer message with fans, explaining that she had needed time to gather her thoughts.

The singer said she understood BLINKs’ disappointment and apologised for potentially making fans “feel even more alone” by not speaking sooner.

Reflecting on the decade BLACKPINK and BLINKs have spent together, ROSÉ said she had hoped 8 August could simply be a day when the group and its fans could celebrate.

“I wanted Aug. 8, at least, to be a day when all of us could smile and be happy, but things didn’t turn out the way I had hoped, and I’m deeply sorry,” she said.

She also thanked the fans who attended the anniversary gathering despite the hot weather and expressed her hopes for BLACKPINK and BLINKs to continue making memories together.

LISA apologises over how the milestone unfolded

LISA also addressed fans in a message following the anniversary.

The BLACKPINK member said she felt sad about how the milestone had unfolded and apologised to fans, acknowledging that the anniversary was meant to be a special celebration shared between the group and BLINKs.

Rather than offer a justification for what happened, LISA focused her message on the relationship BLACKPINK have built with their fans over the past decade.

Her statement followed those from JISOO and ROSÉ, making her the third member reported to have publicly addressed the disappointment at the time.

JENNIE: “There’s really no excuse I can give for that”

JENNIE followed with her own message to BLINKs on 17 August after completing previously scheduled festival appearances.

Writing on Weverse, she explained that she had been thinking about the anniversary and was saddened that she had not been able to properly speak to fans about how she felt.

“These past 10 years have given me some of the most special moments of my life, all because of you,” JENNIE wrote.

She went on to directly acknowledge the disappointment surrounding the milestone.

“Our 10th anniversary should have been a moment where we could just celebrate and be happy together, and I’m sorry that instead, some of you were left feeling disappointed,” she said. “There’s really no excuse I can give for that.”

JENNIE thanked BLINKs for supporting BLACKPINK throughout the past decade and said she would continue growing and doing her best to return the love the group has received.

BLACKPINK and BLINKs look beyond the anniversary

The controversy arrived during what was intended to be a major milestone for BLACKPINK and their fandom.

Some online criticism also focused on the members’ demeanour during the anniversary livestream. JISOO received praise from some fans for directly addressing concerns, while JENNIE, ROSÉ, and LISA faced criticism from some netizens over how they appeared during the broadcast.

Those reactions, however, reflected interpretations from online commenters rather than statements of intent from the members themselves. All four have since addressed BLINKs in messages acknowledging the disappointment surrounding the anniversary.

For BLACKPINK, the occasion nevertheless marks 10 years shared with a fandom that has followed the group from their 2016 debut to their position as one of K-pop’s biggest global acts.

As ROSÉ put it in her message to fans: “Although all of us were left with some disappointment, I sincerely want to congratulate us once again. Let’s make many more wonderful memories together.”

items.body: In July, Europe was grappling with extremely high temperatures and, as a result, thunderstorms due to the heat dome over the continent. I live on the top floor of an apartment building and therefore had a particularly privileged view of these natural spectacles. On one occasion, I could see such a storm approaching - a dark wall rapidly pushing toward the city - though it was obvious that the weather front would only graze the city. The gusts of wind were fierce, trees bent under the force of nature, thunder roared, and lightning lit up the sky. But why am I telling you this? Because it fits perfectly with “Equilibrum”, the first track on the new album by the international trio Okuda Müller Hall - Rieko Okuda (Japan; piano), Matthias Müller (Germany, trombone), and Samuel Hall (Australia, drums) - perfectly. At first, the drums just tingle softly; Hall rubs the toms and strokes the cymbals, while Müller delivers an unsettling drone that shifts only slightly. Sometimes it grows louder, then fades again; it literally fluctuates. Then the piano slowly enters the picture, with Okuda attacking the interior of the instrument. Almost imperceptibly, everything grows louder, darker, and more menacing. The thunderstorm is now over you, but only a few heavy drops are falling, symbolized by isolated piano notes. Even though you know you’ll get off lightly, a hauntingly beautiful, fascinating feeling lingers. “Six Lights,” the third and longest track on the album, continues this form of improvisation in a similar vein. Müller, however, forgoes the drone, opting instead for deliberate, sustained notes over which Okuda showers bright piano sprinkles, while Hall works his magic on the dark drums and simultaneously manipulates extended materials. Müller then takes a two-and-a-half-minute break, and when he rejoins the piece, it actually sounds like contemporary European free jazz or like - say - a trippy ECM recording. In general, ³√ (“Cube Root”) combines wide-ranging developments with a finely balanced structure, it’s a perfect showcase of Berlin’s Echtzeitmusik scene, the trio’s music flows organically into a distinct sonic language - multi-layered, crystal clear, a combination of density and openness. The liner notes mention that an “acoustic space of great depth and fluidity unfolds, within which a steady pull develops, drawing the listener ever deeper into this flowing, ever-changing soundscape“. My favorite track on the album, though, is the last one, “Sputnik.” The thunder and lightning of the opener are gone; what remains is the wind - rough, wild, hissing around the corners and producing strange sounds. Rieko Okuda creates a powerful soundscape against which Müller and Hall enjoy a great deal of freedom, and which ultimately proves what they are - in a musical sense: a force of nature. The album ends with a few subtle dabs of piano. Fascinating and stunningly beautiful. ³√ is available as a download. You can listen to the cording here: ³√ by Okuda Müller Hall Email This BlogThis! items.body: Label: Pi Recordings, 2026 Personnel - Henry Threadgill: alto saxophone, flute, bass flute; Liberty Ellman: acoustic guitar; Jose Davila: tuba, trombone; Christopher Hoffmann: cello; Elliott Humberto Kavee: drums. I dig Henry Threadgill’s type of sound, how he orchestrates modern classical, progressive chamber jazz, and avant-garde opaqueness using layers that unfold with meticulously planned coherence and originality. Threadgill’s prominent presence on the contemporary avant-garde landscape has a strong association with Zooid, a tight quintet that has never felt so loose as in Cut You Where You Was . Threadgill is not heading into a new direction here, but the album has plenty to discover and enjoy. On “ Fluoroscope ”, we notice intervallic leaps within a highly contrapuntal environment, which is so characteristic of the saxophonist’s style. With a tight focus on arrangement and composition, the piece also counts on mystifying solos by Threadgill, who uncorks atypical melodies, and guitarist Liberty Ellman, whose acoustic patterns sound just right over the textural oddities generated by cellist Christopher Hoffman, tubist José Davila, and drummer Elliott Humberto Kavee. The three-movement chamber piece “ Bingo ” explores a variety of exquisite feels and moods: “ Bingo Part 1 ” sets elated flute flights against tuba wails, low-key guitar specifications, and somber cello; “ Bingo Part 2 ” features Ellman’s bluesy slide technique as flute and trombone contribute to the exotic, picturesque landscape; and “ Bingo Part 3 ” thrives on motivic alto sax and enthralled mallet drumming. “ Red Admiral Red Moon Rising ” is the album’s centerpiece, clocking in at more than 12 minutes. What begins as a mournful dirge with plenty of delightful detail quickly evolves into a captivating, quirky groove that has its own imaginative way of swinging. Only Threadgill can come up with these rhythmic jaw-droppers, and his dissonant solo here resonates within that narrative thrust. His ability to go against structural norms and jazz conventions is also mirrored on “ Off And On What Happened ”, where the inventive, unaccompanied Kavee shines. Counterpoint and fragmented cadences are injected before the skillful drummer finishes what he had started. “ Lightnin’ ” is another miniature gem, with sax and guitar declaring curious lines in unison and a deliciously offbeat groove underpinning Ellman’s clear yet nonconformist statement. Passion and openness are present throughout the album, and the final result is simultaneously haunting and bewitching. items.body:
For anyone paying attention to Vietnamese or Cambodian pop culture, the past several days have seen a flurry of online commentary in Southeast Asia and beyond about a new music video by Phương Mỹ Chi and DTAP titled 'Thiên đường với người thương', or 'Paradise with my love'. The track is in Vietnamese and follows the conventions of Vietnamese pop, but the music video (MV) features Khmer Krom culture from southern Vietnam, with scenes filmed at Khmer wats (temples), displays of Khmer dance, and a staging of a Khmer wedding. The central characters in the video are a classical dancer, played by Phương Mỹ Chi, and a musician, played by actor Bảo Định, who meet as children, grow up together, fall in love, and get married.

The video presents a wholesome story and celebrates Khmer Krom culture. The Khmer Krom, or lower Khmer, live in the Mekong Delta and are related to the Khmer people of Cambodia. Both were once part of the Khmer Empire, but several factors have shaped a distinct Khmer Krom culture. Starting in the 17th century, Vietnamese populations moved into the Mekong Delta, which ushered in several centuries of cultural mixture. French colonisation and independence movements established a boundary between Cambodia and southern Vietnam that limited movement. And the distinct qualities of the Mekong Delta itself yielded new cultural forms. The Khmer Krom therefore have many folk traditions about which little is known.

Responses to the video have largely been positive, but it has touched a nerve among some netizens who decry the cultural appropriation of Khmer culture by a Vietnamese pop artist. This debate offers insight into the wider geopolitics of Southeast Asia and the trends of contemporary pop in Vietnam.

The release of 'Thiên đường với người thương' has taken place amid vibrant experimentation with folk traditions in Vietnamese popular music. Songs of folk pop or folktronica feature pop singers reclaiming various folk traditions of their parents and grandparents to fuse them with popular music models that circulate worldwide. Phương Mỹ Chi has several tracks that blend southern Vietnamese traditional music with global pop aesthetics. Artists from northern Vietnam do the same: Hoàng Thùy Linh's 'Để Mị Nói Cho Mà Nghe' incorporates elements of Hmong music, and Kiều Anh's 'Lá Ngọc Cành Vàng' folds a short ca trù (sung poetry) tune into an instrumental interlude.

At the same time, the Vietnamese government plays an influential role both publicly and behind the scenes in promoting some artists over others. For instance, in 2013, the government banned public lip-synching to promote genuine vocal performance but later rescinded the ban. More recently, several pop musicians, including Miu Lê and Phương Diễm Huyền, faced criminal prosecution for supposed illegal activity. Any arrest is a warning to other singers, as Vietnamnet recently indicated.

In this context, Vietnamese pop artists must figuratively walk several tightropes in their artistic creation. The first tightrope involves navigating the razor-edged distinction between cultural appropriation and legitimate experimentation in an environment of fickle social media trends and youth tastes. On this, 'Thiên đường với người thương' has done rather well.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by VietQ Media (@vietqmedia)

An article in Cambodia-based The Phnom Penh Post suggests that the music video appropriately “acknowledges” the origins of the Khmer dance and rituals. This echoes Cambodian and Khmer Krom social media posts that relay a sense of pride in seeing Khmer culture represented on an international stage. Vietnamese and diasporic Vietnamese communities also enjoy the video, as VietQ Media has reported.

Social media posts strengthened the case for visual acknowledgement one day after the MV’s release. Phương Mỹ Chi gave her thanks to Trà Vinh University and her dance teacher, Thạch Thị Út Linh, while DTAP released a visual of musical instruments and customs seen in the music video.

The track has not been entirely successful in raising awareness of Khmer Krom sonic culture, however. During one instrumental interlude, for instance, the MV shows musicians playing various instruments of the Khmer classical music genre pinpeat, or ngũ âm in Vietnamese, including the sralai (a quadruple-reed instrument) and Bảo Định playing the roneat ek (xylophone). But the soundtrack contains none of the distinct timbres of these instruments. Instead, listeners hear a rather boring guitar riff. Khmer culture is seen here but not heard.

The second tightrope involves navigating opaque areas of government permissibility. I have no access to specific information about the making of the MV, but the video's wide circulation suggests that it meets government regulations and requirements. The song also upholds the ideals of the recent Resolution 80 on the development of cultural industries in Vietnam, which seeks to promote culture but also manage it appropriately.

Given this environment, it’s no small feat to find fertile middle ground between artistry and policy to successfully represent Khmer culture in Vietnam. This is of paramount importance because of the difficulties today in accessing Khmer Krom music, dance, and rituals. Artists do not often perform outside of the Mekong Delta, with only a handful of performances taking place every year in large cities in Vietnam. Tourists also rarely visit Khmer communities in southern Vietnam, given the lack of infrastructure.

At the same time, murky restrictions often prevent the study of Khmer arts in southern Vietnam. Earlier this year, the very university that supported the MV’s production team would not authorise my Khmer music lessons with staff instructors. This is, of course, the university’s prerogative, and given the long history of colonial and other forms of exploitation, I understand their caution. But my case is not an isolated one among domestic and foreign researchers in Vietnam. And might the commercial use of the Khmer arts by a Vietnamese pop singer also be seen as a form of exploitation?

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Phương Mỹ Chi (@phuongmychi)

The case of 'Thiên đường với người thương' is therefore a complicated one. The song acknowledges, represents, and values the Khmer arts in Vietnam, but at the same time manages and exploits them for commercial and nationalistic ends. But no government can fully control a narrative.

Among the online discussion are several commentators from Thailand who have both congratulated Vietnam for displaying “Thai culture” — thereby completely erasing Khmer and Khmer Krom culture — and remonstrated with Vietnam for featuring “inauthentic” forms of Thai costume and dance. In the midst of a military conflict between Cambodia and Thailand, they have added to the widening culture war between the two countries by bringing Vietnam into it.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by Ben Pham (@bnphm0609)

Pop is never boring, and foreign (i.e. non-Southeast Asian) audiences must start to pay attention to the dynamics that bring these songs to life. 'Thiên đường với người thương' encourages reflection on the interconnected nature of music and everyday life and the shifting tightropes that all individuals must navigate when making artistic decisions. And while certain powers may attempt to control a narrative, the openness of the Internet quickly dissolves that enclosure.

I am therefore optimistic about 'Thiên đường với người thương'. I truly hope that it will generate new interest in Khmer Krom culture and open new doors for Khmer artists to showcase their artistry to new audiences. The paradise of the video, then, may not be romantic love, but may instead be a paradise of visibility. Audibility may well be next.

Written by Alexander M. Cannon. He is Professor of Ethnomusicology at the University of Birmingham. This article benefited from a conversation with an avid consumer of Vietnamese popular culture who wishes to remain anonymous. Their contribution is gratefully acknowledged.

items.body: "There is no such thing as a stranger�s children." - old Ukrainian saying I�ve long been affected, indeed somewhat obsessed, by what�s happening in Ukraine, partly because of one of my favorite bands, DakhaBrakha. I went to Kyiv to see them at the time of the Maidan protests, just after the shooting by snipers of over a hundred protesters. I intentionally didn�t read this album�s booklet notes before listening, so that I could react to it without sympathetic pre-judgement, just as music. It�s strong musically and vocally by any standards, Ukrainian or otherwise. When I did then turn to the notes that translate and explain the songs, I had that rare experience, for me, of becoming moist-eyed. The songs are a mix of traditional and original. They are focused on the abduction by Russia of about 20,000 Ukrainian children who have been taken from their parents in Russian-occupied eastern Ukraine and sent to Russia, in an attempt to turn them into haters of their native land and people. It�s a heinous war crime. Marichka is a Ukrainian-Canadian singer who moves between Canada and her homeland. For this album she�s gathered two groups of musicians, one in each country. Both ensembles contribute vocals and instrumentation, mostly bowed strings, plus some bandura and piano. The group in Ukraine includes Lisa from the destroyed and invaded city of Mariupol, playing a solo on double ocarina; at 16 she was one of the stolen children but managed to return to Ukraine. Daughters of Donbas � co-led by Marichka and singer/bandurist Alina Kuzma, who shares the lead vocal role � is an all-female ensemble in Canada that tours performing these songs. �Foreign Land� is a reworking of a traditional song about the young girls who were sent away to work in foreign households - Marichka�s grandmother was one of these - that can also be taken to refer to the plight of today�s stolen children. The translation goes: A mother packed up her daughter To leave for a strange land To a strange land with strange people Oh, who will pity you, my daughter? Those who will beat me will pity me I'll never again live with you, my mother When, my daughter, should I expect you to come home? When the grass in the garden grows, my mother The grass grew and grew and began to dry The mother was waiting for her daughter to return, and began to cry Did you hear, my mother, how I came to you? How I flew as a bird above your window? How I cooed like a dove? If, my daughter, I could hear you I would open all the doors and windows To let you fly in Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Alina Kuzma, Zo� Santo As befits the song, Marichka�s vocal here is gentle. But in the second track, �Rusalka,� with Alina Kuzma taking the lead vocals, things turn harsh and fierce. A rusalka is a mythical creature, a nature spirit of fields, forest and rivers, that features in traditional ritual songs. The melody of this one is by Zo� Santo and Kuzma, with lyrics drawing on tradition and the composition of Santo and 19thC Ukrainian poet and folklorist Taras Shevchenko. An ominous double-bass drone, chunking strings, a slithering vocal that moves into sections of white-voice fast recitative and expands into a soaring wild cry. The lyrics are very dark, perhaps evoking the hell of the front line: Home a hell of old growth stumps Marsh a mud of memories Don�t get bogged down in these parts Your kind won�t last a day in here While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. A rusalka sat on a white birch, rusalky asked girls for shirts. Long fingers and nails so sharp Tongue forked round serrated teeth Moss grows down beneath her parts Weeds braided from ear to ear While witches still fly, while roosters have yet to crow, Come here, something arises, �neath the oak something walks. �Girls, my friends, give me your shirts. Though I�m thin, give me a thin one.� Here live us the backless ones Many voices of dead sons You are right to quake in fear Send your sinful children here �Who Am I� is a plea of separation and disorientation, the pain and confusion of an abducted child, contrasting �the human in me� and �the creature in me,� like an internalized riddle-song, with the refrain, in English: Who am I for you? Who am I for me? Do you know me? Really know me? �Enchantress,� passionately sung by Kuzma to her own bandura accompaniment, a girl�s lament of the loss of her brave love taken from her by the enchantress, who is an allegory of war, is based on a traditional song and uses that style of melody and lyrics, �Riddle,� sung by Marichka, reworks a traditional riddle song to be the riddles told by the grandfather of a child, 12-year-old Kira from Mariupol, who experienced the death of her father and her abduction to Russia. Her grandfather tracked her down, and brought her back, traumatized, and asked her riddles - as the notes say �to jog her memory, and remind her who she was, where her home was, and of her family�s love for her.� Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �4.5.0� is a military expression for �all�s well� or �all is quiet.� The song is a message, as from a mother, to a stolen child. Marichka�s voice is cherishing: Remember this: I am with you, I am here Don't give up, I'm with you. Don't give up, I'm with you Your hope is my weapon Don't be sad, I'm with you 4.5.0. will be again �breaking into a tearing howl: And when the world's axis breaks When the sky folds like a parchment Out of nowhere her words will come� �and back to fragile reassurance �It's all right, I'm here, I'm here� "Lullaby," based on a traditional lullaby, sung by Alina Kuzma to accompaniment by her bandura and Zo� Santo's viola, starts in gentle lullaby style, but moves to a lament; it's for the stolen children and those who, as the notes put it, 'have been stolen for ever.' Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, Marichka �Remember, I Believe in You� is a powerful piece of harmonizing vocals and slithering strings. Here�s the story it�s based on: Yevhen lived in Mariupol with his three young children. During the siege they lived in a basement bomb shelter for months. One day, Russian soldiers entered their bomb shelter. Yevhen was taken to a filtration camp and separated from his children who were all taken to a hospital and then to Russian summer �camp�. In the filtration camp Yevhen was brutally tortured and forced to sleep standing on one leg. He tried to fall asleep, whispering prayers for his children: �Everything will be fine, I believe in you.� After his release he walked 30 kilometers to the place where his children had been taken but it was too late. They had already been sent to Moscow. Yevhen learned of this after receiving a text from one of his children who had found an unattended device. He traveled thousands of kilometers, crossed the borders of three countries, endured checks, interrogations and danger to reach Moscow and take his children home. All those days he tirelessly repeated to himself, �I believe in myself, I believe in my kids. Everything will be good.� �Another Heaven,� sung by Marichka with the ensemble in Ukraine, is inspired by another heart-rending story: Ilya was 9 years old when his mother was killed by a rocket strike right in front of him. He was taken to a hospital in occupied Donetsk, where 15 pieces of shrapnel were removed from his body without anesthesia. After he appeared in a report on Russian television, Ilya�s grandmother learned his location. She managed to bring her grandson to Kyiv, where he lives now, experiencing missile attacks every night. At age 11, he says that it is up to everyone to fight enemies, to protect other cities, and to build another heaven, where your home will not be destroyed. In 2014, during the Kyiv Maidan protests, Marichka wrote and performed �Red Boots Tango,� using a melody she�d put to a poem by Taras Shevchenko. For this album she sings it again in Ukraine, with the ensemble there adding swirling, classic tango-style strings. Songs of Stolen Children by Daughters of Donbas, BanduraGirl The final track on the album is a solo, recorded in Kyiv, by Anastasiya Voytyuk, accompanying herself on the older, simpler form of bandura that was used by kobzars to accompany epic poetry, and also on the nowadays more well-known big, heavy form developed from it in Soviet times that was made mainly in the piano factory at Chernihiv. Her song, �Soon I Will Be Back,� is based on a poem by novelist, journalist and war crime researcher Victoria Amelia, who was killed in 2023, in the city of Kramatorsk in Donbas, by a Russian rocket. items.body: Palagoma is not only the first release from Nairobi-based label Cool Waters, it also marks the first time German-born, Kenya-based percussionist Sven Kacirek has collaborated with Ogoya Nengo and Olith Ratengo at the same time. Odd Okoddo, the duo of Kacirek and Ratengo, has been performing since 2018, but with the inclusion of the 83 year old Nengo, a singer from the eastern part of the country, there�s an added traditional depth to the music. A 2025 performance shows Nengo�s lifetime of experience singing Kenya�s dodo tradition around 2 and half minutes in (see below). Furthermore, her inclusion on this album allows her and Ratengo to toss the vocals back and forth as they reference their shared roots (Ratengo and Nengo live minutes from each other). Musically, however, the tracks are driven by Kacirek�s Buchla synth, hand percussion, and occasional kit drumming, which serve to buoy the voices without blotting out the music�s origins. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Bara,� for example, begins with the dime-store thwack of a repeated pattern, a stiff juxtaposition to the voices; yet, as the song rolls along, a 4/4 clink appears, then a burbling bass, and finally, what sounds like a xylophone. Layers of synthesized polyrhythms keep presenting themselves with a subtlety almost unnoticeable, until, by the track�s end, it feels organic, as if it�s all been underneath the two voices all along. Palagoma by Odd Okoddo & Ogoya Nengo �Sarah,� perhaps the album�s most intense track, features a lead vocal from Ratengo and tentative, percussive spittles from Kacirek. And while the technology never tries to overtake the vocals, it does sneak up and punctuate the track�s urgency, as edgy distortion sneaks in here and there just as Ratengo�s voice reaches its peak. The term �folktronica� has been bandied about as a way to house the type of music on offer here. In fact, exploratory collaborations such as Chouk Bwa & The �ngstr�mers as well as much of Kampala, Uganda�s Nyege Nyege label house sounds that might be �folktronic� in some way. What�s more interesting and important about this music, though, is how truly global so much of it is while maintaining a deep connection to Africa and its diasporic communities. The music on Palagoma , as well as much of what�s linked above (and available in countless other recent recordings) demonstrates a real willingness for cultures to respond to each other without trampling traditions altogether. Instead, roots become avant-garde and innovations become seemingly thousands of years old. Certainly the inclusion of an 83 year old traditional Kenyan singer only recently making her global debut as she tours with a duo whose instrumental voice is a white male saturated in electronic Kenyan rhythms demonstrates this blurring. The music this trio makes is certainly of the 21st century, but it�s often hazy, sparse, and open, keeping it from a quick sell-by date or confining it to a specific genre. Instead, it�s a beautiful example music as grace.

According to its founder, Eugene Rodriguez, who also sings and plays on the record, Los Cenzontles is a �musical group and non-profit organization, which I founded over thirty years ago.�  As he continues in the album�s liner notes, the group �has a long history of producing projects exploring Mexico�s deep roots and our connections with various traditions that, so far, have included Irish, Louisiana Creole, Cuban, American cowboy, classical, pop, rock, and blues�, the latest of which is
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
. Los Cenzontles translates to the mockingbird, or, from its Aztec root word, the bird of four hundred voices. This is a fitting name for the range of musical diversity represented here.
With songs sung in Spanish, Hawaiian, and English, the concept traces back to the legacy of Mexican cowboys who travelled from California to the Hawaiian Islands to wrangle the long-horned cattle introduced there in the nineteenth century. They also brought the guitar. The 16 tracks feature old Hawaiian songs with new Spanish lyrics, old Mexican songs with new Hawaiian lyrics, new compositions, and traditional Americana. Yet it is an entirely cohesive musical package held together by dense arrangements of ukuleles, guitars, Mexican harp, and accordion.
Sonny Lim & David Hidalgo
Besides their distinctive voices, the headline artists Taj Mahal and David Hidalgo provide the gravitas and musicianship that their long and distinguished careers have earned. According to the liner notes, they were the catalysts behind the project and facilitated the choice of songs, arrangements, and played a range of instruments. On vocals they are joined by Hawaiian natives Gary Haleamau, Sheldeen Haleamau, Sonny Lim, and long-time Cenzontles member Fabiola Trujillo.
Deportee
To give a taste of the sessions, included before the traditional �Fishin� Blues� is Taj Mahal teaching the musicians how to play it. Sung by David Hildalgo,  the lovely �A Matter of Time� comes from the 1984 album
Will the Wolf Survive
by his most famous project, Los Lobos. Another standout for me, �Navegar� features a slack string guitar solo reminiscent of Duane Eddie and one of many tasty lap steel turns by Sonny Lim. Their interpretation of Woody Guthrie's �Deportee� moves into social commentary, highlighting the cruel realities of being a migrant worker in America.
Vaquero Paniolo
Recorded over five days, mostly live in one room at the Los Cenzontles headquarters in San Pablo, California, including the talents of some of their academy�s students, the recording has real spontaneity to it. Arrangements are stretched by improvisations, sometimes by several different instruments on a single tune. The project also represents a great spirit of cooperation and diversity of language, culture, age, and gender. It includes the inputs of musical legends, seasoned pros, and amateurs. The wonderfully rich and often stereotyped musical cultures of both Mexico and Hawaii are represented here with the authenticity of lived experience.
Adios Ke Aloha: Waves of the Same Sea
is a worthy addition to Los Cenzontles� important work. Quoting Rodriguez again, �Culture is a fabric within which we are all woven.�

The musical partnership between Kalaniemi and Alakotila has thrived over a remarkable 35 years, long enough to the Finnish pair to develop a stunning intimacy and telepathy. Kalaniemi is a lovingly melodic accordion player, with a sharp ear for a good tune, building each one into a thing of great beauty, while pianist Alakotila not only supports her but adds enough of his own to help transform every piece into a glistening gem.
There�s a sense of calmness to the work here, a long, sweet exhalation between two instrumentalists who are deep enough in sync to allow seamless improvisation beyond any written score and carry the listeners along with them. For much of the album, it�s just the pair of them, including Kalaniemi�s wordless voice, as on the opener, the tradional �Lyck�nskan.� She does charmingly sing lyrics on the title track, written by Lasse M�rtenson, with the sound there neatly and sparingly expanded with the addition of a string quartet.
Morgondimma
There are several original pieces alongside the tradition, with Kalaniemi�s �Hambo Vid F�bodan� a real standout, and it�s perhaps inevitable on any disc featuring accordion that a Piazzolla tune should be included, brings its own shadows to the whole (�Oblivion�). And, this being Finland, a tango is almost obligatory, in this case Alakotila�s �Tango Berlin.�
Tango Berlin
There�s a gentle, dreamlike quality to so much of this, flowing and mellifluous. The pieces aren�t an arena for showy virtuosity. Instead, the two musicians serve the tune, exploring and genuinely enjoying their performances.
It won�t shake the earth, but it makes for some true listening beauty.

items.body: For an overview of the what, the why, and the where of this music, do read my review of Volume 1 of this series. Essentially, this collection is more of what made Volume 1 so infectious. Yet, what makes this music so fascinating in general, that is, beyond its unswerving ability to fill dance floors, is the fact that these two islands, part of the Paises Africanos de Lingua Oficial Portuguesa (PALOP) regions of the world, are the second smallest African country; Seychelles is smaller. There are only 12 villages on Sao Tom�, lots of rain forest and, not surprisingly, lots of rain. I mention this because one could be fooled into thinking, with music like what�s on offer here, there must have been a music scene larger than there actually was. Not that little was happening, but that less got recorded or released than it might have had there been a city such as Lagos or Nairobi with the studios, labels, and pressing plants to better document it all. The music here, like Volume 1- recorded during Africa�s so-called golden age- is known as Puxa, a complex stew of ingredients from other former African Portuguese colonies mixed with rhythms that, with the help of dancers, can summon spirits or exorcise demons. At least according to some. It�s worth knowing that a 100 years or so ago, the Portuguese banned Puxa dance; it�s also worth knowing they appear to have failed miserably at this silly endeavor. Tucked away in modern Puxa is merengue, Kompas, Soukouss, Benga, and much else. One suspects much of this is coincidental, while other grooves were definitely imported considering both Portuguese rule and the islands� location over the Atlantic from the Caribbean. But don�t be fooled into thinking these two islands don�t have their own thing, as the sounds on this collection show. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s - Pedro Lima Pedro Lima, who has featured in his own Bongo Joe collection, leads a fiery band, complete with choked guitar vamps tussling with a kit drummer as a lead guitar comments from the sidelines on �Sossegado.� Elsewhere, Sangazuza demonstrates what happens when the bass and keys drop out, leaving the drummers and guitars to ride out a groove and drive dancers mad in the process. Check �Sono s� ku� de t�ma� or �Mairo bi cedo� for their ability to place a firm finger on the pulse. Over 15 tracks, the collection shows off multiple guitars weaving and circling one another, with lead and harmony vocals constantly in response, becoming part of the songs� melodic framework. At any given moment, vocals give way as the music unspools and floats on grooves that must have gone on for hours live. Africa Negra�s �Apoi�mos a luta dos nossos irm�os� is one example. L�VE L�VE Vol. 2: Sao Tom� & Principe Sounds 70s-80s by Various Artists In general, what�s on offer here, like Volume 1, was recorded at Radio Sao Tom� e Principe (RSTP), often taped in the courtyard outside at night, and released on cassette or occasionally, vinyl. It captures the joy of post-1975 independence and only fizzled out as styles changed and musicians struggled to make ends meet. Yet, take a quick listen to recent RSTP programming, which features musicians such as Babilonia or Calema, and you�ll still hear Puxa rhythms, showing just how potent the music form this two-island nation is on a global level. And Bongo Joe, who have also released two volumes featuring the above mentioned Africa Negra, have given this music the treatment it deserves, with extensive notes on the country�s history, vintage photographs, and band discographies. items.body: Known for playing with County Joe McDonald, and for her experimental sound band The United States of America, Dorothy Moskowitz came back in 2023 with United States of Alchemy and their well-received release, Under an Endless Sky . In collaboration with avant-garde composer and filmmaker Francesco Paolo Paladino, and poet and music writer Luca Chino Ferrari, Songs of Compassion is eleven songs containing subversive and at times beautiful music, and richly evocative lyrics. Francesco Paolo Paladino and Luca Chino Ferrari | Photo by Maria Assunta Karini Songs of Compassion has two challenges for the listener. The first is the music, called variously avant-garde, ambient, modal, non-linear, and a few more. It is played mostly on pianos mixed in and out of the foreground, sometimes doubled, and sometimes out of phase, joined by strings, woodwinds, synth washes, and steely sounds. Initially disorienting, the music serves to remind us how locked our minds are to Western notions of harmonic movement. It speaks of alternative musical narratives much older and much further away. They are songs that subvert the song: more like Steve Reich than Steve Stills; more like Phillip Glass than Phil Collins. UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY - Pale Wanderer At the same time, there are the poetic yet strikingly contemporary lyrics. �Pale Wanderer� talks about the fact that authoritarianism needs willing accomplices, describing what happens �When you make a deal with darkness.� UNITED STATES OF ALCHEMY (Dorothy Moskowitz, Francesco Paolo Paladino e Luka Chino Ferrari) by Silentes �Charlottesville� (written with the late Joe Byrd) evokes the time not long ago when torch-wielding nazis, proud of the metaphoric Ns on their tunics, chanted the antisemitic tropes paraphrased in Moskowitz�s words, �We�ll be one people, pure of race/No greedy throng could take our place� . Besides the overtly political lyrics, in the tradition of 1960s protest songs, there are also thoughtful meditations on mortality and our place in the universe. The message is high-minded yet sincere and direct. World weary and wise, Moskowitz�s voice inhabits the evocative philosophical lyrics with the authority of a skilled method actor. The melodies unfold like streams of consciousness, rising and falling, not following expected diatonic chord progressions, but honouring, instead, the value of each word. Moskowitz�s piano acts as another voice and sometimes a kind of Greek chorus commenting on the proceedings. The surrounding music frames, creates pulses and dissonances, and shimmers. The return of Dorothy Moskowitz with her renamed project has arrived in a moment quite similar to the times that spawned its predecessor. Political division, unrest, and uncertainty always generate artistic reaction, and United States of Alchemy roared back to life with their epic 24-minute opening track �Under an Endless Sky� in 2023, serving perhaps as an �In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida� for our times. Songs of Compassion continues to challenge how we think about our world. It�s music that defies the song form, while doing exactly what music is supposed to do�enrich the human condition. The Gods Laugh certainly doesn�t disappoint, with the same deliciously amorphous feel that�s defined her other work, drawing on folk, the avant-garde, as well as a sense of religiosity to make the music here, possibly best exemplified in �I Am!�, where she set a poem by John Clare, England�s great nature poet, to a transcendent melody over the constant underpinning of a lulling drone. While the playing revolves around her usual arsenal of viola, harmonium, hammered dulcimer, and piano, along with some percussion, on this album she also adds some drums, bass and synthesizer. The music is often improvised and captured in a single take, with an almost mystical, hushed sensibility that seems to reach through time, as with �I Still Know You are Calling My Name,� where the tune could have been plucked from an old folk song. It�s far from the longest track on the album, but a little pearl of perfection that carries the listener away. Sprigs of Heather by Alison Cotton The Gods Laugh is a memorial of sorts to Cotton�s father, who died in late 2024. There�s a sense of loss reaching across these tracks, most specifically present on �The Final Harvest,� a solemn piece about her father�s last visit to the allotment he loved so much. It�s suffused with tenderness that extends beyond words. Light and darkness bleed into each other across the music, and moods shift. It�s music that happily stands beyond category, with hints of so many things, but ultimately standing as Alison Cotton music, which might well be all the definition it needs. items.body: Those of us who have been digging into Analog Africa�s increasingly formidable releases over the last two decades are well aware of the massive amount of raw, vodun-based Sato and Sakpata-derived funk the label has issued by Benin�s most prolific 1970s-era band, the Orchestre Poly-Ritmo. AA has dropped no fewer than 3 compilations of their heaviest material, as well as a reissue of the band�s first LP, in an effort to give them the international status they deserve. That being said, what might be different about this collection of their music? And who is Antoine Dougb�? Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa As it turns out, Dougb� was a song-conjurer whose mode of musical transfer was slapping his legs in a rhythm known as Cavacha, a groove created by drummer Belobi Meridjo, who was inspired by a train cadence that he worked into a pattern that ultimately spread like a 21st century California wildfire throughout Congolese pop music in the mid-1970s. Dougb�, known as the �Devil�s Prime Minister,� was also a practitioner of vodun who inspired fear in any musician he felt was unsuited to play his music, which is how he landed on working exclusively Poly-Ritmo, as he felt they could nail what he wanted in ways other bands couldn�t. His recording career was brief - 3 albums and a few singles - but as this collection shows, it was potent. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa Because of the era from which this music dates, it�s not surprising that the recording and instrument tones have changed - the guitars have a plastic sheen and synthesizers appear- even if the music remains rooted in the 1970s. Perhaps the influence of the Cuban son is more apparent here than on other Poly-Ritmo collections, especially in the collection�s initial offerings. And yes, Congolese rumba, then shaking all of sub-Saharan Africa to its knees, is present too. �Ma Won Min Towe Leo� is one example. Opening with a bed of synthesizers, the shimmering guitars, tinny, seemingly squeezed dry by the 80s themselves, lock in over relentless high-hat-focused grooves. The guitars finally start firing in different directions midway through, before that synth weaves back in, forming a bed underneath it all. Antoine Dougb� et L'Orchestre Poly-Rythmo De Cotonou 1977 - 1982 (Analog Africa No.44) by Analog Africa �We Tayi Sin Assi Tche� is much more overtly Cuban. With its insistent cowbell, classic, nasal vocal call and response, and tight, repeated guitar figures, its debt to mid-twentieth century Afro-Cuban sons is transparent. Another track, �Djomido Ma Dougbe Tche� rides a groove reminiscent of 70�s-era Franco classic �Liberte.� The pulse is relentless, and the guitar solo repeats a tight repetition of a few notes, driving listeners to ecstasy all the while. However, none of this music is a mere copy of its influences; rather, like so much potent pop coming from the continent at the time, it is a swirl of major influences rendered by local rhythms and vocal phrasing to give it specific identity, in this case, to Benin. Dougb�s musical role on this collection is a bit murky. One of his three albums has a photo of him, fully mic�d behind a collection of hand drums, so perhaps he served as a percussionist/vocalist; this release never explains. He wasn�t a songwriter in the traditional sense. It seems he was more of an instigator and arranger, but his thumbprint was apparently heavy enough to warrant his name on the records he was involved with. Whatever the case, in his brief run as a recording artist, he and Poly-Ritmo produced a handful of driving, Cavacha-inspired grooves that can still wear holes in club floors. items.body: Tako Toki are like desert island musicians who, castaway without their instruments, were forced to construct their own. Lucky for us, they are as skilled in making instruments as they are in creating original songs with which to show off their handicrafts. Un Dimanche � Monaco is the band�s follow-up to their well-received debut, Hirsute Farfelus , with a similar mash of musical styles. Before discussing the music, we need to talk about their instrument closet. They really have built everything they play out of bric-a-brac, odds and ends, and rubbish. I�m not sure from listening which is which, but they call their instruments, in an incomplete list, tassofons, tilofons, and tubofones, clarinuts, didjerimou, and klarbass, and my favorite, kitchenofon. (I will refer to what I hear by the names of store-bought instruments that they sound like.) The most surprising thing for me was how accurate the instruments were to pitch and how good they sounded under the harsh scrutiny of modern recording microphones that have documented a rich, high-quality sound. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki They have also very effectively matched their choice of instruments with the style of music that inspires their compositions. Right off the top, �Yinitza� features a laughing clarinet singing a klezmer tune accompanied by bassoon for the bass, frantic two-time percussion, and the exuberant human yelps found on many klezmer recordings. As on this track, many tunes feature improvisations that show an impressive degree of musicianship. On the cumbia-inspired �Le Cuenta,� the characteristic flute carries the tune, augmented by a Spanish singing chorus, and remarkably rich-sounding Latin percussion. The title track surrounds us with afrobeat woodblocks, shakers, and rattles scattered around the mix. The melody is played on a marimba ornamented with bells and cymbals. Again, the lead player improvises over the tune and often against the beat with jazzy chops. The flute returns on the samba-inspired �Ambiguidade,� and on �Aksum� it traces a trance-like Middle Eastern tune reminiscent of a 60s TV spy-show theme. UN DIMANCHE A MONACO - LP by Tako Toki Full of fun and one of a kind, Un Dimanche � Monaco celebrates our universal love of rhythmic, melodic, and harmonic sounds and the varied, wonderful ways cultures have organized that love in what we call music. At the same time, playing on literal pieces of junk, Tako Tiko reminds us, as we contemplate many mall music shops filled with gleaming wood and brass instruments and countless unused guitars lying in closets, that musicians will always find a way to make music. Sometime in 1986, perhaps in a Paris caf�, Dominique Cravic, a singer, guitarist, and musical archivist, met Robert Crumb, an underground cartoonist, banjo and mandolin player, and jug-band aficionado. Over a few glasses of marc, to continue to speculate, they conjured up the idea for Les Primitifs du futur.  Since then, they have recorded an impossible-to-categorize series of albums, with cover illustrations by Crumb, of which Les Crimes du Mussette is the fifth.
Weird and wonderful, it sounds like they rooted through an attic full of 78 RPM records, scribbled down some arrangements, and then played them on a collection of instruments they found in another attic, including accordion, sax, xylophone, clarinet, banjo, ukulele, theremin, Hawaiian guitar, bagpipe chanter (I�m guessing here), and musical saw.
Ne tirez pas sur le pianiste (excerpt)
The 27 short tracks are mostly voiced by Cravic, who talk-sings in the manner of an everyman Maurice Chevalier. He is often accompanied by the accordion, a customary instrument in the bal-musette style that remains a strong element of the eclectic range of styles they have managed to synthesize. They also include ragtime, jug, French chanson, and, to my ears, skiffle,  just to get the list started.
Ukulele Lady (excerpt)
The liner notes point out that �Les Crimes du Musette is also a gold mine for scholars, a veritable treasure trove.� Exploring the treasures is beyond my scope here, as each tune has a long history. A highlight for me is the humorous �Ukulele Lady� from 1925, which first delighted me on Arlo Guthrie�s 1971 album
Hobo�s Lullaby
. The song has also been covered by Bing Crosby, Peter Sellers, and Bette Midler.
N'oublie pas Gr�co (excerpt)
A more serious item is �N�oublie pas Gr�co� (Don�t Forget Gr�co�)  is a tribute to the legendary chanteuse and heroine of the French Resistance, Juliette Gr�co, who died in 2020. You will also hear old chestnuts like �Fum�e aux yeux� (�Smoke Gets in Your Eyes�),  �Boude pas� (�Take Five�), and �Prive d�amour� (�As Time Goes By�).
This record is a curiosity, but it is performed by serious musicians with total commitment. In this, I was reminded of the similarly indefinable Dan Hicks & the Hot Licks. Long-forgotten music and abandoned styles are given new animation with obvious enthusiasm and care. Speaking about himself and his collaborators, many of whom are in their seventies, Dominique Cravic says, �The young have fire, but we have light.� In its own little corner,
Les Crimes du Musette
shines bright.

Tiny Sun creates tiny songs that give off light and heat well out of proportion to their size. Composed, performed, and produced by Martina Sorbara, Jonathan Goldsmith, and Don Rooke, the record is vaguely Americana, with plucked guitars and ukuleles, chiming keyboards, and the lonesome slide of the guitar.
Vanishment
contains eighteen sparkling miniatures - that take a scant 34 minutes to negotiate - notable for their economy of arrangement and the subtle directness of the lyrics. The tracks glow with Martina�s clear, high, and sometimes fragile voice.
The songs are about loss: lost love, lost confidence, but sometimes about resignation to the enigmatic quirks of the world. The tone of wry fatalism mirrors the fact that this project is the work of many years of collaboration and email exchanges while the trio pursued their musical day jobs. Jonathan Goldsmith is an award-winning composer for television and film, Don Rooke fronts the Toronto roots band The Henrys, and Martina Sorbara is known for folk, electropop, and her band Dragonette.
Kerosene Madrigal
The range of backgrounds leads to many styles, and the record betrays interesting influences. The opening track, �Kerosene Madrigal,� is a sort of miner�s blues reminiscent of Michelle Shocked. The soul-country of �Imagined Love� reminded me of fellow Torontonians Cowboy Junkies, especially the sweet organ. The stoic and twangy �Don�t Fault the Stars for Falling� could have been a Dolly Parton tune.
A Grand Expanse
�A Grand Expanse� has a more ambitious arrangement.  It sounds like the end-credits song from a long-ago film we only vaguely remember. It says everything it needs to in one minute and twenty seconds and exactly 38 words. It is quintessential Tiny Sun.
The entire recording feels like music from a dream, and since no one knows exactly what dream music sounds like, this could be it.
Berceuse
Tiny Sun will perform the entire album at Toronto�s Koerner Hall on May 14, 2026.

But the quest to look beyond their own country's folk music continues. Camilla Hole's main instrument being the soprano sax, the influence of jazz is unsurprising and this is evident in the opening track �Springleik,� signifying a tune used to accompany the springleik dance from the west of Norway. Initially Hole takes the melody with Egil Kalman and Knut Kvifte Nesheim providing rhythmic support on double bass and drums respectively, with the overdubbing of Kalman's modular synth and Nesheim's vibraphone adding colour. But characteristically for this trio, in which assigned roles are never clearly defined or adhered to, things soon start to move around, with Kalman taking up the melody on his bass, playing the melody in unison with Hole, while Nesheim opens things out further rhythmically. As the whole piece takes on a much more improvisatory feel, Hole plays the melody one more time as things draw to a close. Langs by Camilla Hole Trio
